scenes.title: Generative AI Fundamentals and Amazon Bedrock
scenes.narration: Welcome to our first technical module. This slide shows the four building blocks we will connect throughout the course. At the upper left is the foundation model. It gives our application capabilities such as understanding a question, creating text, or producing other supported outputs. Below it is enterprise data. Your documents, databases, and business rules provide the company-specific knowledge that a general model may not have. At the upper right are prompt controls: the instructions and settings that guide how the model responds. Finally, on the lower right is evaluation. We need a reliable way to measure whether the output is accurate, useful, safe, and consistent. Follow the arrows toward the application at the center. The important idea is that a real generative AI solution is not just a model endpoint. It brings these components together so people can use the model responsibly and effectively. As we move through the slides, we'll look at which AWS features support each part of this design, and why you might choose one approach over another in a production application.

scenes.title: What Is a Foundation Model?
scenes.narration: Here is the foundation model lifecycle, moving from left to right. Start with the large and diverse datasets on the far left. A foundation model is pre-trained on substantial amounts of information, potentially including text, images, code, and other modalities. The training process produces a model with broadly useful patterns and capabilities. But the middle box isn't the end of the story. Look at the three options under Adapt for specific use: prompting, retrieval, and additional training. Prompting supplies instructions during a request. Retrieval adds external evidence, for example a relevant policy or product document. Additional training adapts model behavior for supported use cases. These are different ways of applying a base model, with different costs and operational trade-offs. Finally, the application examples on the right include conversation, summarization, and image-related tasks. The row of model examples along the bottom reminds us that there are multiple model families, not one universal best choice. Selection depends on the task, supported features, latency, pricing, and data controls. For the exam, focus on recognizing the requirement before selecting the model or the adaptation technique.

scenes.title: Choose a Foundation Model by Task
scenes.narration: This slide asks us to select a model based on the type of output, rather than brand recognition. Begin with the top row: conversation and question-answering. The examples include model families such as Claude, Llama, and Amazon Nova. This is the kind of workload where instruction following, reasoning, and conversational quality matter. The middle row highlights text generation and embeddings. Those are related but not identical: a text-generation model writes or transforms language, while an embedding model turns content into vectors for similarity search and retrieval. The bottom row covers images and video, with model examples designed for visual generation and transformation. Notice how each row connects a task category to a different kind of model capability. An important distinction is that not every foundation model supports every output modality or every API feature. Availability, access requirements, and pricing can also change by Region and over time. So treat the named models as examples and verify the currently supported options in Amazon Bedrock. The practical lesson: choose the capability and constraints first, then find the model that fits.

scenes.title: Amazon Bedrock
scenes.narration: Now we bring those model choices into the AWS environment with Amazon Bedrock. Look at the left side, where organizational data can come from documents, databases, object storage, web content, and private knowledge sources. An application may retrieve relevant material from those sources so the model can give a grounded answer. In the center is Bedrock: a managed service that provides access to supported foundation models through AWS APIs. It also offers features for building applications around the models, such as knowledge bases, agents, model customization, and guardrails, subject to model and service support. Follow the main arrows toward the right. The application selects and invokes a suitable foundation model, then uses the output in a chatbot, content-generation system, or another business workflow. This does not mean Bedrock automatically knows your private information; the developer still designs the retrieval and permission model. Read the benefits at the bottom as well. Bedrock reduces the infrastructure management required to use many foundation models, while AWS security and operational controls help integrate them into a broader cloud architecture. Think of Bedrock as a managed foundation-model application platform, not as the entire finished application.

scenes.title: Four Amazon Bedrock API Families
scenes.narration: This slide divides Amazon Bedrock APIs into management and inference families. Start on the left with the orange control-plane boxes. The Bedrock management API is used for tasks such as discovering and managing supported model resources and customization features. Beneath it, the bedrock-agent control plane covers resources such as agents and knowledge bases. Now move to the turquoise and purple boxes on the right. The bedrock-runtime API is where an application sends inference requests to supported foundation models. You will see operations such as Converse and model invocation. The bedrock-agent-runtime API is used at runtime for agent and knowledge-base capabilities, including supported agent invocation and retrieval workflows. The central application icon explains the distinction: normal request handling should use runtime operations, while configuration or provisioning belongs in the appropriate control plane. Notice the blocked arrows for 'not for app requests.' This is a reminder not to confuse a management endpoint with the endpoint that actually generates a response. For scenario questions, first identify whether the application is creating or managing a resource, invoking a model, or querying an agent or knowledge base.

scenes.title: Converse API: One Messages Interface
scenes.narration: We are now looking more closely at model inference. The main diagram shows an application request on the left, Amazon Bedrock's Converse API in the center, and a model response on the right. The idea behind Converse is to provide a consistent messages-oriented interface across supported models. Read the request fields one by one: a model identifier selects the target model; system instructions provide overall guidance when supported; messages include the conversation history or user content; and inference configuration controls supported generation settings. Now look at the optional configuration boxes beneath the main path. Tool definitions let supported models request external functions through an application-controlled process. Guardrail configuration adds safety controls where supported, and additional model-specific request fields cover capabilities that are not universal. The response panel on the far right represents the generated content and related metadata returned to the application. The important engineering lesson is that a consistent API reduces integration differences, but supported parameters and features can still vary by model. We must handle failures, permission checks, tool requests, and output validation in our application rather than assuming every model behaves identically.

scenes.title: Bedrock IAM: Least Privilege
scenes.narration: This slide is about identity and permissions, a topic you should never treat as optional for generative AI applications. Begin with the IAM role at the left. That role represents the permissions granted to a developer or to an application workload. Follow the three branches to the middle. One permission group is for inspecting available models. Another is for invoking only the approved models needed by the application. The third covers management of Bedrock resources when that responsibility is actually required. These are separate capabilities, and an ordinary production application may not need all of them. The arrows then lead to Amazon Bedrock on the right. The principle at the bottom is straightforward: do not use root credentials for routine development, and do not grant broad access merely because a service is easy to invoke. Use IAM policies scoped to necessary actions and resources, along with appropriate conditions, and review any model-specific or cross-account requirements. For exam scenarios, ask whether the request is a read-only discovery operation, inference, or a management change, then grant the minimum permissions for that action.

scenes.title: Bedrock Model Access and Cost
scenes.narration: Now we connect model selection to access requirements and financial impact. This slide provides a five-step path across the page. First, choose the AWS Region in which the application will use Amazon Bedrock. Second, verify that the desired model is available and that any required access or onboarding conditions are satisfied. Third, choose the appropriate inference mode for the workload: for example, on-demand usage, supported provisioned throughput, or batch processing. The right option depends on capacity needs, predictability, latency, and supported model features. Fourth, review pricing for the selected model and configuration, because costs can vary with input, output, throughput, and the inference method. Finally, run a small test invocation with the actual application permissions. That test helps reveal access, compatibility, or configuration problems before production rollout. Notice how this sequence builds on the previous IAM slide: model access is not the same as a role having permission to invoke any model. For a real design, verify both service availability and the application's IAM authorization, then measure cost using representative prompts and expected traffic.

scenes.title: Explore Bedrock Playgrounds
scenes.narration: We'll finish this part with a practical way to explore model behavior before writing all the application code. Follow the numbered path across this slide. First, choose the appropriate Bedrock playground and a supported model. Next, enter a sample prompt. The example asks for an explanation of how generative AI can improve customer support. The third panel shows the model response and usage information. The important step is not just reading the answer; it's observing the effects of your input and settings. At step four, change instructions or generation parameters, such as those supported by the selected model, then try the same task again. Finally, compare the outputs side by side. Look at the orange loop along the bottom: iterate and explore. In a real project, use these experiments to understand model strengths and limitations, then capture reproducible prompts and evaluations for your application. Playground testing is useful for discovery, but it is not a substitute for production testing, access control, or automated evaluation. In the next video we'll discuss when model customization, including fine-tuning and LoRA, becomes appropriate.
